latest_articles.title: Towards a Reciprocal Datafication Model: How data flows in our digitally mediated reality
latest_articles.abstract: This contribution explores the deep entanglement of datafication in our digitally mediated reality and introduces the Reciprocal Datafication Model (RDM) as a conceptual framework for understanding how individuals shape and are shaped by data. While data offers opportunities for optimization and participation, it simultaneously reinforces inequalities and power asymmetries, manifesting in phenomena such as surveillance capitalism and data colonialism. Centering the individual, RDM conceptualizes datafication as a reciprocal process across three interrelated flows: the structural flow, which captures socio-technical infrastructures and power relations, the critical flow in which data practices are socially negotiated and oriented towards optimization or surveillance, and the self-relevance flow, where data shapes meaning-making and cognitive processing. RDM bridges individual data practices and broader social structures, while contributing to communication theory by offering an analytically grounded approach to understanding how digitally mediated realities are produced, experienced, and governed, and how individuals navigate emerging inequalities within them.
authors: Alexander J A M van Deursen

latest_articles.title: From Algorithms to Affection: Unpacking the Psychological Mechanism of Emotional Attachment Toward Virtual Influencers
latest_articles.abstract: As virtual human influencers (VHIs) increasingly inhabit social media landscapes, they are functioning not merely as marketing tools but as social entities capable of eliciting user affection. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying emotional attachment to these artificial agents remain underexplored compared to their human counterparts. This study investigates how VHI self-disclosure influences emotional attachment, positing parasocial relationships as a mediator and perceived attractiveness and humanness as boundary conditions. We analyzed online survey data from 540 young adults familiar with VHIs using a moderated mediation framework. The findings reveal a complex dynamic distinct from human interaction: VHI self-disclosure generally hindered parasocial relationship formation unless the VHI was perceived as physically attractive. This suggests attractiveness acts as a requisite gateway for users to accept artificial disclosure as relationally meaningful. Subsequently, parasocial relationships strongly predicted emotional attachment, an effect significantly amplified by perceived humanness. Consequently, self-disclosure indirectly promoted emotional attachment only when the VHI was viewed as both attractive and human-like. These results delineate the distinct roles of VHI attributes: Attractiveness facilitates the initial establishment of a social connection (parasocial relationship), whereas perceived humanness deepens this bond into a meaningful emotional attachment. Theoretically, this study expands the understanding of human–agent interaction by identifying these differential pathways. Practically, it suggests that developers must prioritize high visual attractiveness to make VHI interactions acceptable, while simultaneously imbuing agents with human-like qualities to foster lasting emotional loyalty.
affiliations: Department of Advertising & Public Relations, Hanyang University—ERICA Campus, Ansan, South Korea.
School of Advertising & Public Relations, Hongik University, Sejong, South Korea.

latest_articles.title: The Real-World Effects of Constructive Journalism: A Field Experiment on Climate Change News
latest_articles.abstract: To explore the effects of constructive journalism beyond one-shot experiments, this study utilizes a 2-week constructive journalism campaign on climate change in two regional Danish news outlets. Employing a difference-in-differences approach, news users exposed to the campaign were compared to news users from regions not exposed to the campaign. The constructive journalism campaign yielded more positive evaluations of news coverage, but not on core quality aspects like trustworthiness and balance. No effects were found for emotional responses, response efficacy, and behavioural intentions, but a positive effect was found for self-efficacy, indicating the potential of a constructive approach to journalism.
affiliations: Centre for Journalism, University of Southern Denmark, Odense M, Denmark

latest_articles.title: From platform outrage to institutional consequence: Convergent hybrid media accountability in Morocco
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops the concept of convergent hybrid media accountability (CHMA) to explain how informal digital criticism is translated into institutional consequence in Morocco’s hybrid media environment. Moving beyond the view of accountability as an internal professional virtue, the article argues that where formal bodies are fragile or distrusted, citizens use platformed publics to initiate scrutiny from outside media institutions. Drawing on a pragmatist mixed-methods design – combining a survey of 205 social media users, eight semi-structured interviews with journalists and editors, and process tracing of nine accountability episodes (2022–2025) – the study finds that online outrage only matters when it crosses a threshold of convergence . This bridging moment occurs when informal claims gain legitimacy and procedural uptake through two linked mechanisms – amplification and legitimation, then escalation and formalisation. Findings reveal an empowerment paradox : the most active users report high efficacy but also perceive strong institutional resistance. The article concludes that platform acceleration and emerging digital-content regulations have intensified both the speed and selectivity of accountability in Morocco. Ultimately, this study offers CHMA as a de-Westernising, potentially transferable framework for analysing how media accountability operates in hybrid media environments characterised by media pluralism and managed political asymmetry.
affiliations: Laboratory of Language and Society, Ibn Tofaïl University, Kenitra, Morocco

latest_articles.title: How social media produces “Cheap Europe”: Digital Balkanism and the politics of creator mobility
latest_articles.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate how socioeconomic unevenness becomes visible, often recoding structural inequality as consumable value. This article introduces the concept of digital Balkanism to explain how platformed travel content reworks long-standing intra-European hierarchies. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 108 English-language YouTube videos about Bulgaria, we identify five recurring frames: cheapness-as-freedom, therapeutic pastoralism, discovery, managed difference, and platformed epistemic authority that are recognizable conventions of platformed travel that often operate across other peripheralized destinations. While these frames are not distinctly Balkanist, we identified two higher-order structuring logics that render their articulation in this corpus specifically Balkanist: conditional Europeanness and off-white Europe, which position Bulgaria as “European” yet persistently deficient, and “white” yet conditionally so. Digital Balkanism therefore operates less through overt denigration than through the conversion of this conditionality into epistemic and platform value. The article extends critical platform and decolonial media scholarship by theorizing othering within Europe rather than across a simple West/non-West divide.
affiliations: Syracuse University School of Information Studies, NY, USA

latest_articles.title: The “Netflix Look”: Moving image aesthetics as data under platform logic
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines Netflix’s industrial model through the framework of platform logic, arguing that the data-centric approach it adopts in the production of moving images alters the creative process. The result is a conceptual shift from shooting a film to capturing an image. Bridging platform studies and film theory, I build on David Bordwell’s poetics of cinema, which conceives the production process as a negotiation between institutional constraints and creative intention. Analyzing the Netflix Partner Help Center as a primary document, I argue that it reflects a departure from this traditional dynamic and that Netflix conceptualizes moving image production as a data capture process. I conclude that this transformation reflects a broader data logic that extends beyond Netflix to the production of contemporary moving images.
affiliations: Department of Film Design and Directing, Gaziantep University, Gaziantep, Türkiye

latest_articles.title: Formerly Incarcerated People as Professional Writers and Publishers
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines a publication initiative that aims to recognize formerly incarcerated individuals as professional and technical writers, challenging traditional notions of authorship, expertise, and community publishing. Its goal is to broaden the scope of professional and technical writing to include the voices and perspectives of those who are often marginalized in such discussions.

latest_articles.title: When Past Hurt Meets Present Care: How Family History Shapes Adult Caregivers’ Communal Coping With Siblings in Their Caregiving for Parents With Health Challenges
latest_articles.abstract: This sequential, explanatory mixed-methods study explores how adult caregivers’ perceived family functioning and unresolved hurt toward siblings from childhood are associated with their present-day communal coping (CC) with their siblings and caregiving outcomes. Study 1 tested a hypothesized moderated mediation model using survey data ( N = 776). The results indicate greater childhood family functioning (consistent with hypotheses) and unresolved hurt (counter to hypotheses) were associated with more CC with siblings. CC, in turn, was associated with less flourishing and greater caregiver burden and sibling resentment. Considering the unexpected positive association between unresolved hurt and CC, Study 2 involved semi-structured interviews with adult caregivers ( N = 30) about their experiences enacting CC with siblings despite residual hurt. The findings suggest unresolved childhood hurt toward siblings often stem from challenging experiences, including neglect and abuse. In addition to impeding sibling CC, unresolved hurt can also complicate efforts toward CC (or render them dysfunctional). This study underscores how childhood experiences have an enduring effect on CC with siblings decades later, especially if past family issues are left unresolved.
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara, USA

latest_articles.title: Generational differences in responses to disinformation: from ‘vulnerability’ to interpretive strategies
latest_articles.abstract: Generational differences in responses to disinformation have attracted considerable attention, yet are rarely comprehensively theorised and are often examined with the help of surveys or behavioural data designs. Such designs tend to frame audience engagement from the perspective of ‘vulnerability’ or ‘resilience’ and offer limited insight into how audiences interpret and negotiate contested claims in everyday communication. In this article, we develop a more elaborated conceptualisation of generational differences and propose to understand disinformation not as a set of factual errors to be corrected but as a communicative practice that involves interpretation and interaction. We then examine generational differences in responses to disinformation in three European countries: Serbia, Poland, and Romania. Drawing on 18 focus groups conducted in April-May 2025, we analyse discussions prompted by four disinformation examples per country, two related to the war in Ukraine and two related to LGBTQ issues. We distinguish between three main types of interpretive arguments: those anchored in textual and presentational cues, those drawing on prior knowledge, and those that move toward broader associative narratives. We show that younger participants rely more on text-based scrutiny, older participants more often reframe the materials through personal experience and wider moral and political narratives, while middle-aged groups sit in between. This suggests that generational differences cannot be reduced to differences in susceptibility or media literacy but are grounded in different approaches to argumentation and interpretation.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Closeness and Well-Being in Older Adulthood: A Dyadic Daily Diary Study
latest_articles.abstract: Relationships are central to well-being. Relationship closeness, which measures interdependence, remains underexplored in older adult couples managing chronic health conditions. In a sample of 146 distinguishable dyads consisting of individuals with chronic back pain (ICBPs) and their spouses, the current study explored the role of own and partner closeness for daily well-being. Additionally, to contextualize ICBPs’ daily experiences, their daily symptoms were assessed as a moderator for these links. Couples completed up to 30 days of end-of-day diaries reporting closeness, affect, and their physical symptoms. Using multilevel models guided by the Actor–Partner Interdependence Model, we found that on days when both ICBPs and spouses reported greater closeness, they experienced higher positive affect and lower negative affect (actor effects). Similarly, partners’ closeness was associated with individuals’ own higher positive and lower negative affect (partner effects) in both ICBPs and spouses. Notably, spouses’ daily affect was more strongly associated with ICBPs’ closeness than their own, suggesting spouses’ heightened susceptibility to ICBPs’ experiences. Contrary to hypotheses, ICBPs’ daily symptoms did not moderate closeness–affect associations for themselves; however, ICBPs’ symptoms moderated partner effects for spouses’ negative affect. Simple slopes analyses revealed that ICBPs’ closeness was beneficial (i.e., decreased negative affect) for spouses across low, average, and high-symptom days; the strength of these associations decreased as symptom levels increased, but remained significant. Findings underscore the importance of dyadic perspectives in understanding well-being in older couples coping with chronic illness.

latest_articles.title: Metáforas de la Comunicación Organizacional en la Academia Latinoamericana: Un Diálogo Norte-Sur
latest_articles.abstract: Teniendo en cuenta la existencia de una episteme latinoamericana en el ámbito de la comunicación, caracterizada por un pensamiento crítico y una perspectiva subalternizada, y respondiendo a las llamadas a la descolonización de este campo, proponemos, en este ensayo, propiciar un diálogo disruptivo/constructivo entre los estudios de comunicación organizacional del Norte y del Sur, centrándonos en las metáforas de la comunicación organizacional. Ponemos en diálogo el marco seminal de Putnam et al. (1996) con los discursos contemporáneos de las personas académicas latinoamericanas en el campo de la comunicación organizacional. Esto da como resultado una tipología de cinco metáforas primarias —transmisión, conexión, coordinación, diálogo, representación— y cinco metáforas complejas. Esta tipología ofrece una reinterpretación contextualizada y matizada del marco importado de Putnam et al. (1996) que destaca la importancia de la metáfora de la transmisión. Además, incluye una dimensión teleológica para cada metáfora como elemento clave de la heurística en uso.
affiliations: Escuela de Comunicación, Universidad de Manizales, Caldas, Colombia
Département de Communication Sociale et Publique, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM), Canada

latest_articles.title: Smartphones, Peer Relationships, and Depressive Symptoms: A Six-Year Growth Model of Adolescent Mental Health
latest_articles.abstract: From a media psychology perspective, understanding how digital behaviors influence mental health requires attention to individual differences and changes over time. This study examined longitudinal associations among smartphone use, peer relationships, and depressive symptoms using six waves of the Korean Children and Youth Panel Survey 2018 (KCYPS 2018), a nationally representative panel of South Korean adolescents (N = 2,460; ages 10–15). Multilevel growth modeling distinguished between- and within-person components of smartphone use and peer relationships. Higher average smartphone use and within-person increases in smartphone use were associated with higher depressive symptoms. More positive peer relationships were associated with lower depressive symptoms at both levels. Although within-person fluctuations in peer relationships did not consistently moderate the association between within-person smartphone use and depressive symptoms, this moderating role changed over time. Specifically, more positive-than-usual peer relationships showed an increasingly pronounced buffering pattern in this association across adolescence. Gender differences were also observed: girls reported higher baseline depressive symptoms, whereas boys showed steeper increases over time. These findings demonstrate the importance of distinguishing between- and within-person processes and considering adolescents’ social contexts when examining associations between smartphone use and mental health.

latest_articles.title: Colonial continuity and the African film industry: A comparative political economy of structural reproduction
latest_articles.abstract: African cinema produces at scale and commands global cultural prestige, yet captures a fraction of its economic potential. The film sector generates only USD 5 billion from an estimated potential of USD 20 billion; piracy accounts for over half of potential revenues in two-thirds of African countries; Nigeria operates 68 cinemas for a population of over 200 million; and former cinema houses in Burkina Faso, host of the continent’s most celebrated film festival, are now market spaces. This paper argues that these conditions persist because the political-economic arrangements organising African film industries were established under colonialism and reproduced through successive institutional forms, including postcolonial state film companies, structural adjustment and digital streaming platforms, serving global capital at the expense of African producers and audiences. The colonial continuity thesis, developed through Mosco’s framework of commodification, spatialisation and structuration, provides the mechanism-level explanation for this persistence. Applied comparatively across Nigeria, Ghana and Francophone West Africa, three contexts selected for meaningful variation in colonial history, state film policy tradition and industry form, the framework reveals convergence that no country-specific explanation can account for, extending Ngwenya’s challenge to critical political economy by specifying the colonial structural logic that class-based analysis leaves unaccounted.
affiliations: University for Development Studies, Tamale, Ghana

latest_articles.title: Deadpool as a lumpenproletarian film
latest_articles.abstract: In this essay, I incorporate the notion of the irony bribe with classical Marxist literature to illustrate how the first Deadpool film functions as a lumpenproletarian film. I argue that Deadpool’s meta-commentary mockery of the superhero film genre and other media texts functions as an irony bribe because its disavowal of the film’s superhero consensus allows Deadpool to enjoy a childish individualistic spectacle that disregards politicized collective action. To illustrate this point, I split this essay into two parts. First, I outline how capitalism’s economic development conditions the lumpenproletariat to be susceptible to the bribe. I also use Lacanian psychoanalysis to illustrate how capital within neoliberalism bribes the lumpenproletariat with the immaterial profit of enjoyment. Second, I use this Lacanian psychoanalytically informed Marxist framework to examine how Wade Wilson (pre-Deadpool) already existed in material conditions that made him vulnerable to the bribe. Afterward, I examine how Deadpool uses his mutant powers as an irony bribe to enjoy his individualistic disavowal of superhero ideals within the film. Finally, I outline this essay’s contributions to examine lumpenproletarian media and calls for future research.

latest_articles.title: Message Framing and Causal Attributions Shape Public Reactions to Parkinson’s Disease: Evidence from China and the United States
latest_articles.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a visible and stigmatized condition that is often misunderstood by the public. Drawing on attribution theory and cross-cultural health communication, we investigated how causal explanations for PD (biological vs. environmental risk factors) and message framing (individual-focused vs. group-focused) shape emotional and behavioral responses across two cultural contexts. In Study 1 (N = 260), Chinese participants read vignettes describing either an individual with PD or a broader population affected by PD and reported their sympathy, anger, willingness to help, and donation intentions. In Study 2 (N = 168), a parallel experiment was conducted with U.S. participants. Across both studies, biological explanations elicited greater sympathy and generally stronger supportive responses than environmental-risk explanations. Consistent with our predictions, individual-focused messages generally produced stronger responses among U.S. participants, whereas group-focused messages tended to produce stronger responses among Chinese participants. These findings highlight the importance of attribution-sensitive and culturally informed communication strategies for reducing stigma and promoting support for people living with PD.
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

latest_articles.title: “They Call Us Cheaters”: Exploring Stigma Management Communication Strategies During GLP-1 Medication Use
latest_articles.abstract: As GLP-1 receptor agonist medications become more popular, conversations surrounding the medication’s use are becoming increasingly more complicated. Emerging research suggests that individuals taking these medications often feel stigmatized. However, understanding how individuals manage stigma through communication is less explored. Using stigma management communication theory, the current study seeks to better understand how individuals communicatively manage stigma surrounding GLP-1 medication use. A reflexive thematic analysis of interviews with GLP-1 users (n = 34) suggests that individuals evaluate their interpretations of both their own self-stigma and the public’s understanding of GLP-1 and engage in various different stigma management communication strategies in response. These strategies, while effective for stigma management, may inadvertently contribute to ongoing stigmatizing discourse surrounding GLP-1 use.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin
Department of Humanities, New York City College of Technology City Tech

latest_articles.title: Narratives of transparency: how do commercial and non-commercial providers of research information legitimize the datafication of research?
latest_articles.abstract: The datafication of research has immensely expanded the possibilities for creating more metadata regarding research practice and performance. This has supported the growth of research information produced by commercial and non-commercial providers based on digital infrastructures including bibliometric databases, research information systems, and analytics services for the scientific community and beyond. In this paper, we ask how the providers of research information legitimize the need for the datafication of research and thus for their tools by looking at the providers’ narratives of transparency and how they differ according to their business model. Based on 22 expert interviews with employees of commercial and non-commercial organizations, we show that there are three narratives – demonstrating research performance, improving research, and supporting research governance – that build on distinct meanings of transparency, implying particular understandings of research practice and performance, which influence how research is made accessible and assessable through the metadata and analytics services the organizations provide.
affiliations: Governance in Higher Education and Science, German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies, Hanover, Germany
Institute for Media and Communication Studies, Free University Berlin, Berlin, Germany

latest_articles.title: The work of digital inclusion: exposing the digital labour of community workers fostering digital participation
latest_articles.abstract: This article presents findings from a national-scale research project that worked with disadvantaged communities across Australia to examine digital inclusion in low-income families and the role of social infrastructure (e.g., schools, libraries, charities, government services) in supporting digital participation. Drawing on data collected in interviews and community workshops in an outer urban community with significant socio-economic challenges, we illuminate the digital labour of community sector workers who routinely act as digital mentors. These workers support family members who often lack access to digital devices and services along with the requisite skills to use digital technologies to perform everyday tasks, such as helping families to contact telecommunications providers, access government apps, and apply for jobs or rental leases online. In light of our results, our study extends the concept of digital labour to include work undertaken in the service and advocacy of digital inclusion in community contexts. Specifically, we articulate the activities, challenges, frustrations, and costs (in time and resources) that characterise digital inclusion support of low-income families, often beyond role expectations. In doing this, we seek to expand understandings of digital labour both as a category and concept. Overall, the article demonstrates that digital inclusion initiatives must not only accommodate the intersecting socio-cultural needs of low-income families, but include appropriate support and resourcing for community workers performing critical digital mentoring work.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
latest_articles.title: Augmenting Technical Editors: A Quasi-Experimental Study of AI-Assisted Copyediting
latest_articles.abstract: Technical editing research has examined the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, yet empirical studies on their effectiveness remain limited. This quasi-experimental study investigates whether an AI-assisted tool improves copyediting performance and explores editor perceptions. The study compared 33 students’ editing performance with and without AI assistance. The results showed that an AI tool provided selective benefits, failing to raise overall correction rates but improving detection of AI-flagged errors. Perceptions varied by skill level, with stronger editors finding AI to be more distracting than helpful. The authors consider the teaching implications of this study and suggest that future research should test the effectiveness of various AI tools across different technical content types.

latest_articles.title: When journalists and scientists sit down to talk: Juggling audience expectations in interactional science podcasts during the COVID-19 pandemic
latest_articles.abstract: Given the growing relevance of podcasts in science communication, especially science journalism, this paper analyzes interactional science podcasts from a dramaturgical perspective. Scientists and journalists face conflicting expectations from different audiences, ranging from professional peers to a ‘general audience.’ Nevertheless, their interactions tend to be relatively harmonious. This paper addresses this puzzle and asks how journalists and scientists juggle audience expectations in different roles. It is based on a qualitative analysis of 15 episodes of the prominent German podcast ‘Coronavirus Update,’ sampled through mentions in metajournalistic discourse during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany. The analysis shows that conflicting expectations require a certain variation within role constellations: actors speak as (co-)moderator, (co-)expert, and as a representative of the audience. The constellations are stabilized through mutual support of each other’s self-presentation, but also the intentional withdrawal thereof in risky situations. Unpacking those interactional dynamics, shaped by audience expectations, helps to understand the social dimension of science journalism and its emerging practices, such as podcasting.

latest_articles.title: Exploring Geographic “Reach” in Local Visual News: A Mapping Approach
latest_articles.abstract: The importance of local news outlets having a physical presence in and understanding of the geographic places they serve is widely established in academic literature. Yet vast and sparsely populated coverage areas—such as those in regional, rural, or remote Australia—can challenge the feasibility and practicality of this ideal. This study explores the use of mapping methods to visualise and assess geographic patterns of visual news coverage published by two news outlets in communities in two different states, focusing on photographs as spatially anchored indicators of journalistic presence and attention. Specifically, we identify the locations of 701 news photographs published across the two outlets over a constructed year and then plot these on maps using a point-based approach. We then experiment with different ways of mapping these locations and reflect on the challenges of these approaches. In doing so, we highlight the value of using heat maps to more clearly reveal disparities in coverage density across the outlets’ self-defined “news zones”. Our findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of mapping approaches in identifying under-served areas and in complicating the issue of a news outlet’s “geographic” reach in the digital era.
affiliations: School of Media and Communication, RMIT University
School of Communication and Creative Arts, Deakin University
Department of Communication and Media Research, Université de Fribourg

latest_articles.title: Does Office Type Determine Gendered Campaign Messages?
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how candidates’ gender shapes campaign messaging across different branches and levels of political office. Prior research offers mixed evidence on whether women are more likely than men to emphasize communal traits and women-related policies, often because gender effects are examined without fully accounting for institutional context. We address this inconsistency by foregrounding the role of electoral institutions. Building on strategic stereotype theory, we argue that gendered campaign messaging is a strategic response to office-specific incentives and expectations. In particular, we expect gendered appeals to be more prevalent at lower levels of government than at higher levels, and more pronounced in legislative than in executive races. We test these expectations using an original dataset of 46,966 official campaign booklets issued by all candidates competing for district-based executive and legislative offices in seventeen national and local elections in South Korea from 2000 to 2022. These booklets are legally standardized, page-limited documents distributed to voters and provide a rare opportunity to compare campaign messages across offices while holding the communication medium constant. We measure gendered messaging through candidates’ use of relational language and women-related policy terms. The results show that female candidates emphasize relational identities and women’s policy concerns more than male candidates. Crucially, the magnitude of this gender gap varies across institutional contexts. Gender differences are larger in legislative contests than in executive races and increase as elections move from national to subnational levels.

latest_articles.title: Professors laughing at themselves too much: the negative effects of instructor self-defeating humor
latest_articles.abstract: Humor researchers have examined instructor self-disparaging humor in the college classroom, but not the use of a similar (yet more intense) construct known as self-defeating humor. Using Benign Violations Theory (BVT) as a framework, this study examined how instructor self-defeating humor impacted students’ perceptions of (a) affect, (b) instructor credibility, and (c) appropriateness, while controlling for moderation effects of (d) students’ own humor orientation (HO). One hundred fifty-seven students (N = 157) completed an online survey in which they reported their perceptions of an instructor’s use of self-defeating humor and the above-mentioned variables. Results indicated that instructor self-defeating humor use was negatively related to important instructional communication concepts such as instructor affect (r = -.28), instructor competence (r = -.32), and instructor appropriateness (r = -.59). Furthermore, students’ humor orientation demonstrated no interaction effect between instructor self-defeating humor and any of the outcome variables. While some instructors feel comfortable making fun of themselves, findings suggest that they should avoid self-defeating humor during instruction because students may find them less credible, less appropriate, and less likable overall. Ultimately, instructor appropriateness is a better predictor of student perceptions of affect and credibility than instructor self-defeating humor.

latest_articles.title: Concessionary storytelling: epistemic freedom in Zimbabwean anti-extractivist documentaries
latest_articles.abstract: Scholarship in African communication and media studies increasingly focuses on how Africans use mediated communication to enact epistemic freedom in environmental contexts. Contributing to this line of inquiry, this article analyzes how Zimbabwean civil society organizations challenge state and corporate narratives that cast mineral extractivism as essential to national development. We examine the Centre for Natural Resource Governance, a civil society organization that produces anti-extractivist documentaries on the negative consequences of mineral extraction for rural and Indigenous communities. Advancing the concept of “concessionary storytelling,” we argue that these documentaries enact epistemic freedom by rendering mineral concessions—government contracts granting corporate access to land, labor, and resources—intelligible through community-grounded knowledge of their promises and pitfalls. We develop this argument through an analysis of three documentaries addressing platinum, diamond, and lithium concessions. Our analysis shows how community testimony and audiovisual evidence are organized through recurring dialectics of order and rupture, resettlement and displacement, and sustainability and degradation. Ultimately, this article opens new avenues for analyzing the role of mediated communication in concessionary politics across the Global South.

latest_articles.title: Manifesting company culture: exploring mission statements and their role in shaping game industry workplace cultures
latest_articles.abstract: We argue that corporate mission statements, as dual-purpose documents that externally communicate an organization’s values and goals to the public while internally communicating the organization’s identity to its workers, are a useful window into the inner workings of the games industry. To demonstrate this utility, we examine statements posted to the Riot Games website: The Riot Manifesto (2014–2018) and the Our Values statement that replaced it in 2019. We approach our analysis as a close reading grounded in feminist media studies, linking the underlying messages embedded in Riot’s statements to broader issues in gaming cultures. We focus our case study to statements made before and after the publication of Cecelia D’Anastasio’s (2018) investigative article for Kotaku, “Inside the Culture of Sexism at Riot Games,” where current and former employees described Riot’s workplace as a “bro-culture.” Our goal is to demonstrate that mission statements warrant serious consideration as ideological documents that play a role in shaping workplace cultures and influencing who is (or is not) seen as “belonging” in the game industry.

latest_articles.title: Interdependent Autonomy: How Digital-Native Media Adapt to Compound Constraints in Flawed Democracies
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates how digital-native media adapt their practices, organizational models, and community relationships when operating under the compound constraints characteristic of flawed democracies. Using a mixed-methods design structured around a case study of La Silla Vacía and Colombiacheck, two Colombian digital-native media outlets, the research integrates a mapping of 46 outlets in the Colombian digital ecosystem, content analysis of 701 articles published by both outlets (189 in depth), and 18 interviews with media ecosystem actors. The analysis identifies four interrelated adaptive dimensions, structural, methodological, territorial-digital, and relational, that respond to specific tensions between immediacy and rigor, digital reach and territorial presence, editorial independence and financial sustainability, and community engagement and journalistic objectivity. These dimensions converge in the concept of interdependent autonomy, the central theoretical contribution: editorial independence is preserved not despite but through the strategic diversification of alliances with other media, academia, civil society, and international cooperation. The findings demonstrate that in flawed democracies adaptation operates as a constitutive process, where compound constraints catalyze innovations that transcend the Colombian context for the understanding of journalism under democratic fragility globally.

latest_articles.title: The few, the loud: platform-mediated articulation of conspiratorial discourse by political elites on X and Facebook
latest_articles.abstract: Despite growing concerns about the role of political elites in producing and amplifying conspiracy theories, little is known about which politicians engage in this behavior, how prevalent it is across countries and platforms, and what ideological patterns it follows. We address these questions by identifying a narrow set of elite conspiracy entrepreneurs who disproportionately produce conspiratorial discourse, challenging the bounds of acceptable debate across three European democracies. Using gradient threshold analysis, logistic regression, and close reading, we analyze a manually annotated sample of posts by political elites (N = 702) in Belgium, Finland, and Poland to identify conspiracy entrepreneurs, characterize them, and examine their cross-platform communication. Results indicate that conspiratorial discourse is driven by a narrow set of predominantly far-right politicians, who generate higher engagement than their colleagues, despite comparable following and posting rates. Conspiratorial discourse also differs across platforms, with Facebook enabling more fully articulated conspiratorial narratives and X favoring more fragmented, context-dependent communication. These findings illuminate how political elites cultivate epistemic crisis and how social media platforms may algorithmically reward conspiratorial content by providing tools for politicians to generate engagement.

latest_articles.title: Reclaiming African Values in the Face of Anti-Globalization Discourses: Do African Leaders Leverage X Formerily Twitter to Showcase African Values and Drive Regional Unity?
latest_articles.abstract: Grounded in value theory and African conceptualizations of values, this study examines how African heads of state use X (formerly Twitter) as a diplomatic platform. It analyzes how African values are articulated in leaders’ digital diplomacy. Based on multipurpose and multilevel sampling 1,443 posts from 13 African heads of state examined through the Discourse-Historical Approach (DHA). African leaders’ X engagement was categorized into four groups based on their posting frequency: high, moderate, minimal, and inactive. Seven thematic pillars were identified: Unity, Solidarity and Social Cohesion; Conflict Resolution and Diplomacy; Democratic Governance and Leadership; Spiritual Connection to Nature and Environmental Protection; Religious, Cultural Tolerance and Respect; Indigenous Knowledge Production; and Heroism, Independence, and Self-Reliance. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Kenyan President William Ruto emerged as dominant actors who leveraged X to assert Africa’s diplomatic agency and counter antiglobal narratives. Presidents of Democratic Republic of Congo and Lesotho were inactive. Discursively, the leaders employed nomination, predication, and argumentation, perspectivization, and mitigation strategies. The study calls for African heads of state to actively engage in and project African values to advance the continent’s interests in a more equitable global order.

latest_articles.title: Role, Position, and Control: Questioning Generative Artificial Intelligence’s Place as a New Actor within Strategic Communications for National Advocacy
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) as a new actant within a compound socio-technical arrangement in the field of strategic communication for national advocacy during wartime. Innovatively combining Actor-Network Theory and Bourdieu’s social field theory, the study analyzes how GenAI technology was incorporated into Israel’s ad hoc national advocacy field established during the ‘Iron Swords’ Israel-Hamas conflict (October 7, 2023–2025). Through semi-structured interviews with 15 strategic communication professionals who used GenAI for advocacy purposes, the study explores how this technology is perceived, positioned, and integrated into professional workflows. The research reveals that while GenAI functions as an efficient and loyal personal assistant that enhances creativity and productivity, professionals strategically position it in the middle stages of the creative process rather than as a front-facing actor. This positioning stems from their concerns about professional status, creative authenticity, and low credibility. The findings contribute to understanding technology adoption in crisis communication and reveal the complex power dynamics that emerge when disruptive technologies enter established human professional fields.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
latest_articles.title: Book Review: Augmentation Technologies and Artificial Intelligence in Technical Communication: Designing Ethical Futures by Duin, Ann Hill, & Pedersen, Isabel DuinAnn HillPedersenIsabel. (2023). Augmentation Technologies and Artificial Intelligence in Technical Communication: Designing Ethical Futures. Routledge. 259 pp. $54.99paperback. ISBN: 978-1032263755.
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and augmentation technologies are rapidly reshaping how humans work, communicate, and construct knowledge.In Augmentation Technologies and Artificial Intelligence in Technical Communication: Designing Ethical Futures, Ann Hill Duin and Isabel Pedersen (2023) claim that technical and professional communication (TPC) practitioners must become central contributors in shaping the ethical, pedagogical, and sociotechnical futures of emerging technologies.Drawing on a variety of theories including posthuman rhetoric, human-computer interaction, data literacy, AI ethics, and (most notably) Rude's seminal work in "Mapping Research Questions in Technical Communication," Duin and Pedersen depict a holistic vision of TPC as a field uniquely prepared to articulate the social, cultural, and political implications of emerging technologies and "provide direction for future practice and collaboration" (p.3).The book comprises three sections, each containing chapters that begin with an overview of the concepts discussed and key questions to consider.Duin and Pedersen argue that our responsibility as TPC practitioners (specifically scholars and instructors) must expand from explaining technologies to shaping how they operate, are understood, and affect individuals Book review

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
latest_articles.title: Knotworking With Artificial Intelligence: A Case Study of Emergent Student User-Experience Composition With AI-Assisted Cocreation
latest_articles.abstract: This case study examines how technical communication students used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in user-experience (UX) design via Figma. Over a semester, they engaged with Figma Jambot, AI plug-ins, and other GenAI tools. Reporting on the findings from students’ individual and team reflections, the authors explore how students used AI-assistance in UX work. Using activity theory's knotworking, the authors study how students articulate GenAI as object, tool, genre, text, and person. In functioning as a boundary object, AI helped to coordinate team workflows and translate design ideas. Then students employed rework strategies to refine designs. Finally, the authors reflect on implications for AI-assisted UX design as a cocreative process.

latest_articles.title: How does political efficacy condition clicks on politics? Understanding information-selection behavior in algorithmic feeds over time
latest_articles.abstract: This study uses political efficacy to explain individual differences in selecting political information on algorithmic feeds. Combining survey data and 186 Dutch individuals’ usage histories of Google Discover, a fully algorithmically curated feed, we examined both within-person changes of information-selection behavior over time and between-person differences conditioned by political efficacy in three aspects: the proportion of political information selected by users, exposure diversity as manifested via sources, and proportion of negative political information. While we did not find any longitudinal change conditioned by external efficacy on information-selection patterns, we found that internally efficacious users are more resilient to prevalent concerns about algorithms’ negative influence on political information consumption and exposure diversity. We observed their stable proportions of political information consumption and consumption from increasingly diverse sources over time. Alarmingly, there is a growing divide in exposure diversity between less and more efficacious users over time. Altogether, our study not only highlights users’ agency in navigating algorithmic environments but also underscores the importance of empowering users with account of different vulnerabilities.
affiliations: Amsterdam School of Communication Research (ASCoR), University of Amsterdam , Amsterdam,
Institute for Information Law (IViR), University of Amsterdam , Amsterdam,

latest_articles.title: Of Networks and Nests: Digital Social Reproduction, Identity, and Support Among Latin American Mothers
latest_articles.abstract: Based on interviews with Latin American mothers in Denmark, this study introduces “digital social reproduction” to conceptualize the invisible, gendered communicative labour through which mothers sustain transnational kinship, build local support networks, and navigate the digital-by-default welfare state. Findings show that linguistic and digital assumptions shift translation and coordination work onto mothers, revealing gaps in ostensibly universal digital infrastructures. Mothers’ everyday digital practices sustain family and community life, generating affective value while becoming entangled with platform datafication as sensitive information is routed through third-party tools.The paper calls for more inclusive digital infrastructures and stronger institutional support for migrant parents.

latest_articles.title: Unpacking Symmetrical Communication: Navigating Polarization During the COVID-19 Crisis and Beyond
latest_articles.abstract: Aiming to address research gaps in symmetrical communication, a conceptual cornerstone for understanding reciprocal communication (i.e. the mutual, back-and-forth exchange between organizations and publics) and relationship management, this study adopts a publics-first perspective to examine how participants navigate polarized perceptions surrounding COVID-19. Drawing on 40 qualitative interviews, we identify two broad domains of strategies: depolarizing and non-polarizing. Depolarizing strategies include identity-focused (e.g. identity transcendence) and issue-focused (e.g. information source diversity) strategies. Non-polarizing strategies include distancing and avoiding, targeted education, and conservation. By centering publics’ interpersonal dynamics, the study reveals the microlevel cognitive and relational mechanisms through which symmetry is enacted in polarized contexts, which could serve as crucial foundations that enable public relations scholars and practitioners to conceptualize and engage in symmetrical engagement during polarized differences. This study advances theory by identifying multi-faceted dimensions of symmetry, adding nuances to the symmetry spectrum, and specifying actionable pathways for reconciling differences and bridging divides.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Extra-Familial Intergenerational Contact in the Contemporary United States: Exploring Its Frequency, Nature, and Correlates
latest_articles.abstract: Some major studies conducted over the last forty years suggest that intergenerational contact between younger and older adults (i.e., those aged 70+) in Western contexts is scarce. However, the phrasing of questions asked in these studies leaves open the possibility that intergenerational contact might not be so rare. In Study 1 ( n = 399), we surveyed young Americans about the frequency and characteristics of their intergenerational interactions. In Study 2 ( n = 278), we surveyed a separate sample of young Americans to assess the quantity and communicative quality of their contact with older people, gather information about their intergenerational relationships, and gauge their attitudes towards aging. In Study 1, 42% of respondents had at least one friend aged 70 or older and over 60% had had contact (typically face-to-face) with an older adult during the previous week. In Study 2, the quality and quantity of contact were associated with the endorsement of prescriptive age-based stereotypes, both directly and indirectly via perceptions of common ingroup identity. Moreover, quantity and quality of contact predicted the affective responses younger adults had at the thought of growing old, and their sense of efficacy about doing so. Our results suggest that the state of intergenerational relations in the United States is less dire than some might believe, and that high-quality contact with older adults is associated not only with less negative stereotypes but also younger people feeling both less troubled by and better able to cope with their own aging.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Seeing I to I Makes Sparks Fly: Daily Diary Investigation of I-Sharing and Relationship Quality
latest_articles.abstract: I-sharing (i.e., the perception that one shares the same subjective experience) with a romantic partner positively predicts relationship satisfaction and perceptions that one’s partner knows one’s true self (i.e., perceived partner true self knowledge. The current work extends the research on I-sharing in romantic relationships by investigating whether daily fluctuations in perceptions of I-sharing with a romantic partner positively relate to daily romantic relationship outcomes such as relationship quality (i.e., relationship flourishing and satisfaction), perceived partner true self knowledge (PTSK), and perceived compassionate acts towards one’s romantic partner. The current work also investigates whether these relationships are independent of Me-sharing (e.g., perceiving one has similar personality traits with one’s partner). The study included a cross-sectional intake survey ( N = 204), followed by a daily diary component ( N = 162, K = 850). Perceived I-sharing frequency does have positive relationships with all the aforementioned romantic relationship outcomes, independent of Me-sharing. These results suggest that daily perceptions of I-sharing frequency are positively associated with several distinct daily aspects of people’s romantic relationships, such as the satisfaction and the sense of fulfillment people derive from a romantic relationship.

latest_articles.title: Institutional realism in media culture: How disability journalism education reveals structural limits of cultural change
latest_articles.abstract: Media institutions systematically exclude disability perspectives despite decades of advocacy and educational intervention. This article examines why cultural transformation efforts fail to penetrate professional media practice, extending Mark Fisher’s concept of ‘capitalist realism’ to reveal how institutional realism operates: we can imagine transformed practitioners but not transformed institutions. Drawing on critical autoethnographic analysis of two contrasting disability reporting education initiatives, an intensive community-partnered program and widely-distributed industry guidance, I demonstrate how professional socialisation functions as a mechanism of cultural reproduction, systematically neutralising educational gains through reification processes. While both interventions demonstrably transformed individual practitioners, neither disrupted what Jacques Rancière (2004) terms the ‘distribution of the sensible’ that determines whose voices become audible in media discourse. This case contributes to critical theory by specifying how institutional realism lets institutions appear to embrace cultural change while containing it. The analysis reveals a depth-versus-scale paradox: interventions intensive enough to transform how practitioners see disability cannot be scaled, while interventions that scale reach only those already disposed to change. It specifies two frameworks: the distinction between epistemic transformation and behavioural modification, and the mechanism through which newsroom routines reify ableist assumptions as professional competence, and positional disability expertise as optional specialisation rather than core.

latest_articles.title: Local in Name Only? The Impact of Ownership and Newsroom Proximity on Local and Original News Coverage
latest_articles.abstract: Local news plays a crucial democratic role by representing communities and reporting on place-based issues. Yet structural shifts such as chain ownership and the consolidation of local newsrooms risk diluting this local focus and increasing reliance on duplicated content. This study presents the first national analysis of local news authenticity in the UK using 465,105 articles from 360 outlets (2020–2022). We operationalise authentic localness using measures of geographic fidelity, coverage distance, and content duplication, and model how these vary by ownership and newsroom proximity. Our results show that corporate ownership reduces geographic fidelity and content originality, while increasing coverage distance, and that newsroom distance compounds this. Our findings demonstrate that ownership consolidation and newsroom centralisation jointly disembed journalism from communities, transforming local news from place-based reporting into networked content production.
affiliations: Institute for People-Centred AI, University of Surrey

latest_articles.title: Media rituals and cultural authorization: Negotiating representational legitimacy in the Super Bowl halftime show
latest_articles.abstract: National media rituals are key sites where cultural representation and legitimacy are publicly negotiated. This article uses cultural authorization to explain how institutions, media discourse, and mediated representations of audience and community reception define who can legitimately represent the nation within these events. Drawing on symbolic boundary theory and media ritual scholarship, the study analyzes coverage of Bad Bunny’s selection as the Super Bowl LX Halftime Show headliner. Using qualitative media discourse analysis (October 2025 to February 2026), the article identifies four recurring dynamics: institutional authorization through market legitimacy, boundary contestation through authenticity claims, counter-ritual formation, and community recognition. These dynamics show how media rituals transform programming decisions into struggles over national representation. The article contributes by specifying cultural authorization as a mechanism through which symbolic boundaries become publicly consequential in mass-mediated events. It argues that media rituals function as authorization infrastructures where market logics, political discourse, and mediated reception claims shape the terms of legitimate representation.

latest_articles.title: Building Deep Data Through Screens: Princeton-SMART for Mobile Communication Research
latest_articles.abstract: This article introduces Princeton-SMART, open-source screen-capture software designed to generate deep data on mobile communication behavior. Princeton-SMART unobtrusively collects screenshots and on-screen text from Android devices at short intervals in naturalistic settings. We describe a research pipeline for secure data collection, preprocessing, and analysis, drawing on over 1.5 million screenshots contributed by U.S. job seekers over 6 weeks. We demonstrate how job-search activities can be identified using vision-language AI models and methodological considerations encountered during the process. We conclude by discussing opportunities and practical implications for integrating Princeton-SMART into mobile communication research.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin
Screenlake, Inc., San Mateo, CA, USA
Department of Politics and School of Politics and International Affairs, Princeton University

latest_articles.title: Smartphone-Based GenAI and the Ruralization of Indian-Language News
latest_articles.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of smartphone-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the editing and increasing representation of rural news in Hindi-language speed news in India. As an innovation, speed news refers to the recitation of news summaries by presenters at an accelerated pace across mobile, television, and digital platforms such as YouTube. Drawing on the anthropological conception of “ruralization” and fieldwork in northern India, I argue that smartphone-based GenAI enables small, rural actors working mainly with mobile phones to more effectively condense and edit speed news stories. Smartphone-based GenAI tools such as ChatGPT help package raw speed news stories into pithy, punchy sentences that resemble a form of kahawat (“saying”) or sutra (“aphorism”), thereby striking cultural chords with Hindi-language news audiences, particularly in rural India. This improved news-editing process also facilitates the steady production of speed news bulletins, contributing to the deeper ruralization of Hindi news. The commentary concludes with a brief reflection on the potentials and pitfalls of smartphone-based GenAI in India.

latest_articles.title: Unmasking the making of a hero: analyzing Aamir Khan’s fandom in China
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates Aamir Khan’s popularity in China as a distinctive case of transcultural stardom. It argues that his reception is shaped not only by the circulation of Bollywood cinema but also by the ways his films align with Chinese aesthetic preferences and social values. Survey findings show that most respondents had watched his films and admired him as both a skilled actor and a socially engaged public figure. Khan’s appeal appears to rest on the convergence of artistic credibility, moral seriousness, and culturally meaningful storytelling. The study contends that his transnational popularity strengthens Indian cinema’s soft power and informs debates on market strategy, star studies, and cultural exchange. More broadly, it suggests that cinema can function as a medium of education, social reflection, and cross-cultural influence when grounded in emotionally resonant, relevant narratives, and it opens new avenues for understanding the reception of Indian cinema in China.

latest_articles.title: The Effects of Online Harassment of Scientists on Bystander Scientists
latest_articles.abstract: Scientists who share research on social media increasingly face harassment, which is visible to many bystanders, including other scientists. We report a preregistered experiment testing how exposure to such harassment affects bystander scientists ( N = 846). Drawing on social identity approaches, we argue that bystander scientists may react similarly to directly targeted scientists. Results show that exposure to harassment increases anxiety and risk perceptions but does not reduce willingness to engage in science communication; it slightly increases perceived trustworthiness of targeted scientists. Presumed influence shapes some of these effects. Shifting attention to bystanders, we highlight broader societal consequences of harassment against scientists.

latest_articles.title: Empowering mpox prevention through agency: risk and control mechanisms in gay and bisexual men
latest_articles.abstract: Despite the decline in cases, the ongoing mpox outbreak that started in 2022 remains a public health concern. Due to its disproportionately high risk on gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, there is an urgent need to develop tailored, culturally sensitive health messaging for these marginalized populations. Drawing on agency assignment and locus of control (LOC) research, this study examined the effectiveness of agency assignment using infographics in communicating risk and control to gay and bisexual men, empowering them to take protective actions. An online experiment (N = 402) with a 2 (agency of transmission: human vs. virus) by 2 (agency of protection: human vs. external) design showed that assigning visual-textual agencies to distinct entities influenced corresponding agency perceptions. Perceived human transmission agency predicted higher perceived ingroup risk, while perceived human protection agency predicted higher internal LOC and lower external LOC. These risk and LOC perceptions were positively linked to self-protection and community support intentions. The findings extend the literature on health risk messaging for marginalized communities through the agency assignment perspective and suggest the need for practitioners to highlight human agency and address systemic barriers in risk prevention.

latest_articles.title: Monsters, magic, mediality: Tabletop role–playing games as mediatization processes
latest_articles.abstract: Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) are often thought of as an analog medium. But their recent renaissance (fueled by the emergence of actual plays and the subsequent increase of online game sessions due to the COVID-19 pandemic) shows how entangled TTRPGs are and have been with the process of digitalization – and that they are better understood as a hybrid medium in general. Understanding TTRPGs this way leads, in turn, to the understanding of role-playing as a cluster of mediatization processes between its different parts, be it players and game masters, narrative and rules, or even reality and fiction. This paper thus analyzes TTRPGs’ mediality and its relationship to other media (computer (games), boardgames, actual plays and the role of the players) to bring various academic disciplines and different branches of game studies into dialogue with one another through the focus on TTRPGs.
affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Security, University of Applied Sciences St. Pölten, St. Pölten, Austria
Department of German Studies, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria
School of Humanities and Cultural Studies, University of Wuppertal, Wuppertal, Germany

latest_articles.title: Amplification, Contestation, and Toxic Interactions with Protest News: How Social Upheaval Reshapes Dynamics between News Organisations and Their Audiences
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines audience-media relations in the context of protest coverage, testing how dynamics of news media amplification and contestation in social media compare between legacy and alternative media. Empirically, we use difference-in-differences models to analyse the effects of the 2019 Chilean protests and a subsequent political agreement on audience-media interactions. Additionally, we probe such interactions as spaces for the expression of negative emotions, directed to media outlets as toxic replies. To this end, we apply pre-trained machine learning models to identify toxicity in user comments. Our dataset includes over 21 million posts mentioning 22 Chilean news organisations during a six-month period spanning three months before and after the protests. The findings show overall increased interactions with both media types after the outbreak of the protests, with distinct patterns of response: alternative media was more amplified while legacy media was more contested, reflecting on broader patterns of public media criticism. These results underscore the audience-media dynamic as a foundational element in how protests are portrayed and collectively interpreted.
